titleStmt.title: Interview with Donald J. Mark, June 2004
titleStmt.author: Christopher R. Riley

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Donald J. Mark was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Well, thank you for allowing me to interview you today.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: I need to know your full name, rank, and date of birth.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Donald J. Mark

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: . . .and your rank?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I was a sergeant, in the Marine Corp.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: . . .and your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What branch of service did you serve?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: United States Marine Corps

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What was the name of the company you were in?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I was in a couple, but uh, I was in a couple, but I ended up in the second battalion, eleventh marines.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How long were you in the service? (during WWII)

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: 25 months in World War II

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How did you get involved in the WWII, by voluntary enlistment, drafts, etc?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I enlisted in the Marines.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How old were you when you entered the war?

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What was the location of your first battle?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Okinawa

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Please describe the condition or state of affairs in the United States in relation to the world at that time.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Oh, the United States was at war with Japan, Italy, and Germany Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: When and where was your first battle or engagement?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: April 1, 1945, Okinawa

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Please describe the military tactics employed at the Battle of Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: The first Marine divisions, uh-- marched across the all, and cut it in half moved north, secured the northern part of the island, and then went south to relieve the army then secured the southern part of the island.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What do you think helped you to survive the Battle of Okinawa or the war in general?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: My mother’s prayers.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did you encounter any viral outbreaks?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Uh, you know like, diseases, colds, something like that.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Oh, I had malaria.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Today, what do you remember the most about the war?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I guess when the atomic bomb was dropped, and we were training to go to Japan-- that probably saved a lot of lives.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did you ever meet Douglas MacArthur?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What was the most disappointing situation that you encountered during the war?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Kinda give me a hint I don’t know how to answer that.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Things that you expected that you wanted to happen, but did not happen.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Perhaps staying in China longer than I, would have liked after the war.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Why were you required to stay in China?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: The Marines were sent to China to make sure that the Japanese surrendered, and repatriate them back to Japan; which we did. We acted as a buffer between the naturalist and the communist in China.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok, were there any prisoners of war?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: From where? Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: From Japan.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Japanese, uh-- didn’t surrender; we had very few prisoners in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok, what is you current occupation?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I am a retired Supreme Court Judge for the State of New York.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: What is the most heroic activity of which you engaged or witnessed in the war?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I guess when we repealed the Benzie attack from Japanese soldiers.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Can you please describe or expand that?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: We were headed to the top of a hill, and the Japanese had kind of a Benzie attack at night, which we repealed.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How many soldiers were involved?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I couldn’t give you an exact account, but the Marines were on one side and the Japanese on the other.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Do you feel that the war positively or negatively affected your life?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Positively.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Well, I ended up with a GI bill, and I was able to go to a college, and law school.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, that was nice

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: It worked out very well.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Is there any thing specifically you would like to have included in this interview? . . . in the museum?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Well, I grew in a time when patriotism was, uh-- virtue, and uh-- and there weren’t many people who were trying or dodging the drafts. People were enlisting; they wanted to fight for their country . . .and it was a good time.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Is there any word of advice to upcoming soldiers.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Just train as well as you can, to be as prepared as you can for combat.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Is there anything else you would have changed in life during that time.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Uh, what do you mean by that? Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Is there anything else that you would like to have changed during that time of war, if you could have changed it?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Well, that concludes the interview. Thank you. . . Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: . . . Oh, you asked about some violent acts, and I thought about the time I was on perimeter defense. And, well, I was connected to another Marine, by telephone, he said to me “Mark check out, uh, 10 o’clock there-- looks like there’s Japanese solider out there.” So I’m watching this figure walking, and all of a sudden three Japanese soldiers almost stepped on top of me, I hadn’t seen them approaching me, So I fired two shots at each one, I had 8 rounds in my rifle, I fried each one real fast, they thought they had hit a machine gun nest.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok!

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I thought you would like that story a little bit better than the attack.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Yes sir, thank you. Do you have any other ones?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Yeah, the attack I told you about, when they came up a hill, we killed about ten Japanese soldiers.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Yes sir, you told me about that one.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: So, uh, like uh, what about your wounds.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Oh, yeah, one time I was, uh, blown through the air, I was hit by an artillery shell--I was blown through the air and ended up with shivers of shrapnel in my rear end.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok,

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: . . . but it didn’t hurt

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok, where was that?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Okinawa,

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Have you ever heard of the story that says, “you never hear the one that hits you, because the artillery shell travels faster than sound?”

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Yes, sir Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I never heard this, I was flying through the air and I was watching my other marines running, they heard it, they were running. The line came closer to me, so I didn’t hear it, so I was flying through the air. And uh, then I started having bumps on my rear end, it lasted for weeks

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Euh.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: And they started pulling shrapnel out of my rear end, but that eventually subsided. It wasn’t a real serious one.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did anyone else get injured along side of you?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No, I was the only one.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I guess I was in the wrong place.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How long were you in the hospital?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I wasn’t in the hospital for that. I just kept going to the sick bay. And they kept on pulling out the shivers of shrapnel. But actually after that I was cured. I had a fungus infection in my feet, I was in the hospital for 35 days.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, ok. Did you have any broken bones?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Well, that was good.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Ha, ha, yeah

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How high in the air did you go, do you know?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I went awfully high though, because I could see the Marines below running for cover.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh-- was in the night or in the day?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: It was just at dusk.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, ok. How often did you go to sleep?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: We slept, uh-- it was called “half on, half off”, we slept half of the night and watched half of the night. Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, okay. How did you eat?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: We ate rations; they were called “C” rations and, uh-- “B” rations.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: And they are like the letter “C” and the letter “B”?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: “C” were in cans and “B” were in a box.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, okay. Were there hot meals or cold?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Cold.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Okay, were there any hot meals at all?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Uh--sometimes, at the back of the lines or when we went to a rest area for a couple of days, were they gave us, what they call 10:1 rations, which were a lot better rations than.. . We use to put, uh, sand or dirt, in uh “C” rations cup, and put gasoline in there and light it, used that as a heater.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did you like, eat any wild berries or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: At one time when they could not. . . , during the rainy season they could not drop food to us. We were eating, uh, small tomatoes, fields, farmer’s fields

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How did you get to Okinawa,. . . like boat, plane?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: We went, we had, uh, I was in the 1st Marine division, we had 3 practice landing on Guadacanal. And then we went, uh, from Guadalcanal to Okinawa. It took us 35 days on a LST.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok what is a LS. . .

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: LST stands for (L)anding (S)hip (T)ank.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, ok! Do you know what kind of LST it was?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I think all it was a LST.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Were there plenty of artilleries with you?

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Not on the ship, no.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: It was just troops and tanks.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How did you get more ammunition? Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: They brought it up to the front lines.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, ok. Did you have plenty of ammunition?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Yep!

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, ok, that was good.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: We didn’t run out of that.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did the U.S. government support you good?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok, well, uh-- How were you remembered, I mean, received back at home?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Well, there weren’t any parades or anything, because I did not comeback until, well, after Okinawa. I think I told you I went to China for 10 months.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: So, I didn’t come home, for ten, the war was over for about 10 months before I came home.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: There wasn’t a parade or anything. My parents were sure glad to see me.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Did you have a family while you were at war? I mean like married?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: No, no, I was only 18.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I remember now.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I had my mother, father, and 2 sisters, they wrote to me.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Do you feel that the WWII veterans were treated better than the Vietnam veterans?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Definitely!

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Okay. How (why).

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Probably was the war, that the country was prepared, the country wanted to fight WWII, because we were attacked, at Peril Harbor. In Vietnam the country was not behind the Vietnam vets. It was a war that, uh-- the country did not want, completely different story from WWI. Riley, Christopher

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Compared to WWI veterans?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: That was a good war too.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I mean I think, because of the. . . , because we were fighting, weren’t attacked, but we were fighting for something.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: How was WWI compared to WWII veterans, which one was better or greater, treated when they got back home?

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: That’s kinda, probably about the same answer.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: I wasn’t around for WWI, because my father was in WWI, and they were treated well.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: That was good, ok, well. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: If you need anymore I will be here.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Ok

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Good luck, Christopher.

sp.speaker: Christopher R. Riley
sp.p: Thank you, good bye.

sp.speaker: Donald J. Mark
sp.p: Good bye!
